utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Kovacic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zirdum.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we adjourned when you were describing the situation in the area of Gacice where you had been assigned. You told that you were there until the end of the conflict and the function you had. You also mentioned the fall of Bobasi after you arrived at the position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more question about this. The BH army, did it win a better strategic or a perhaps a tactical position after the fall of Bobasi, after they came in the area? Better condition in terms of the control of the town or rather the part of the valley, and better if they wanted to cut the valley into two?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, they improved the position in that part very slightly, but they came nearer the town and therefore began to present a greater risk for the population in the centre of the town, that is the most densely populated part of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you worked as a journalist in 1992 and the former half of 1993, and then as an IPD officer, you had access, at least from time to time, to different types of information exchanged within the HVO, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a direct access to information, but indirectly, yes. Being a journalist, yes, I received various information or rather in -- there were press conferences in other places where media were involved. Yes, I would get in touch with the different sort of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you were assigned military tasks, that is, after you were sent to the front line, you did not attend press conferences any longer, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever get any instruction or perhaps learn of an instruction indicating that the objective of the HVO, or rather the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, that is, the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was the secession from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never issued any instruction that might suggest something that the army was to do. Soldiers, of course, needed to have many things explained to them, including the objectives of our fight even though it was quite evident that we are only fighting for defence. But during periods of peace, people wanted to get a grasp of the whole situation, of the situation as a whole, and they -- it had to be talked about with them. But there was never any hint of such an instruction or any sign whatsoever that secession was the objective, the goal of the HVO struggle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get or learn of any instruction supporting or requesting ethnic cleansing, that is, persecution of other ethnic groups or the evacuation from those areas?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I was the assistant for IPD, such things were never the subject of any discussion, that is, it never occurred to anyone to discuss possibly the expulsion or eviction of anyone or transfer of anyone. All that we took was that the Croat people needed to define and ensure an equitable position for themselves in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now cover two or three things that we mentioned under miscellaneous, that is, item 4 in our summary. You did quite a number of stories during the first part of your work that we talked about, and you spoke to a great many people. Did you ever have a chance to talk to people who had been released from their detention in the building of the cinema?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people did you approach, asking them to give you a statement about it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were coming out and signing some paper, and as they were coming out, I asked them for an interview, each one of them. I know that only a few refused to because they were simply reluctant to speak for television; others were simply shy of it and did not feel at ease about speaking for television. But all the others, yes, made a statement, gave a statement to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you in some way sum up their statements?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to ask them how they had been treated there, and they all said that they were treated decently. Others felt the need to call upon the Croat people and the Muslim people and the armies of both peoples to try to resolve political misunderstandings as soon as possible, because they had brought about all that had happened. Many of them were calling upon their friends, inviting their friends, telling them that nothing could affect their friendship they had regardless of what had happened, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now go back to something that you said in the beginning. At that particular time, did you believe that people like you thought that it was to be just a short-lived episode and that people would go on living as they did before?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how many people believed that. But I do think that the majority of people still thought that it was going to be just a brief episode, that there was a minority of those who thought that it was a conflict which had to go on. Most people still believed that, yes, it was just a clash which could be resolved by political negotiation because, after all, there were all sorts of negotiations going on. However, time showed that negotiations were not enough to bring that to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about how internees were coming out of the cinema and that they were signing some paper. Was the Red Cross, the International Red Cross, there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember, but I think they were there or around, because they had already arrived and they were somewhere there. I don't know if one can see them on the tape, but they were in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the contacts that you had, because you came to the office every day -- to the building every day because that is where your office was, did you know about what was going on in the building and the treatment of those people? And did those statements tally with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in touch with those people every day, because there were many of my friends there. So I saw them every day, brought them food or a change of clothes, whatever they needed. I went to their families, visited them, to let them know that everything was all right, not to worry, and so on and so forth. I mean, I was in touch with them all the time. There were no incidents at all -- rather, there was one incident when two internees began to argue, had an argument between them and got to, I think, fisticuffs. But then somebody separated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But apart from that one incident, you don't know of any other?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see any other incident, nor did I hear about any, because had there been any, I would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that place look like a camp, or did it have a different aspect? How would you describe it, in view of its various features, the regime that existed there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when one uses the word "camp," I mean, it sounds horrible. But it did not look like a camp at all. There were no wires or any strict regime or any inadequate regime that governed the place. The conditions that existed there were really used to the maximum so that the interned people could function there as much as they could. I suppose for the first day or two, before I came there, it was very bad there. But as I could realise how they were resolving matters in those -- discussing the WC or other things, that is, certain facilities were open, that people could go freely. I heard from a friend of mine that just the first two days were hell because it was too hot and stuffy and what not, but then everything was opened up, everything was solved, that food had begun to arrive, and communication and contact with families. Then it worked. There was a very liberal regime. We could all go there and talk to our friends who were there, take cigarettes to them, and such like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned, though, that the first two days were bad. Just a moment. Bad because of the objective circumstances, the accommodation, the limitations of the building, or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let the witness give the evidence as to why the conditions were bad in the first two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why were those first two days bad?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was a very small area, that cellar, and there were just too many people. And unless -- until people realised that it was overcrowded and that there had to be some other solution. I wasn't there during those first two days, but then on the staircase I saw a friend on the staircase and he asked me to bring him a blanket. So I went to his home, saw his family, said that he was all right but he needed a blanket. That is, people simply were not prepared for that. They didn't know what they might need there. But later on, as the time went by, people realised what they needed and they were getting things then. The regime became very liberal and quite normal; that is, the conditions that existed there were really used in an optimal manner. Of course, the building is a far cry from a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Zirdum, could the internees receive visitors, their friends or families who would bring them things?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Wives came, brought food and gave them. On the staircase, they would meet or in the doorway they would meet, give them food. Or I went to their homes and would bring them too food or whatever, I mean to those people that I knew, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in those contacts that you mentioned, your contacts with some internees, did you have to do it on the sly?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I moved around freely, and they also moved around freely in some parts, that is, in the passages or WC. So we met freely. All the doors were open and one could enter freely any of those rooms. And they could move from one room to another, that is, they could walk around and communicate quite freely, and of course, everybody had a space of his own, some area of his own and I don't know what they did there. But at any rate, people could move around, and even on radio and television, we had a telephone and some came to call us, and then everybody would want to talk to us and they would say, yes -- we would let them, but -- say yes, but do it slowly. That is, people wanted to let-- needed to let their families, their wives and children, to let them know that they were quite all right, just to -- and I felt, I sensed, that that was a need that they had. So regardless of what otherwise the rules might be, I just allowed people to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come to the telephone and call the television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one more question about this. Did you see what was the army, whose were the troops which guarded the entrance into the building or around the building?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building, there were the military police, the lads with white belts, and I didn't really know whose they were or what. But they were always very correct. I would come in and go out, they never stopped me. They were not disagreeable. It was quite an easygoing atmosphere. I knew some of them. I didn't know some of them. I didn't know who they belonged to. All I knew is that they were military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would kindly ask for a private session for a couple of questions where witness would not like to use a name of his friend publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, during the first days of the conflict, could you please describe very briefly the situation in town. Was there order or was there chaos? Could you say that very briefly?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the first days of the conflict, it's very hard to describe the situation because throughout those three days, I was in the basement, but it was terrible. There was a lot of shelling, and we focused on putting our shelter in order because, in the meantime, sandbags had arrived, and all the men from the building, Muslims and Croats as well, went to put the sandbags against the windows. I heard that there was chaos in town, that all sorts of things were going on, but I, in those crucial and chaotic days, I did not see for myself what was going on. Later on when I came to the television, I could see what the situation was, but that was when the chaos was subsiding and things were getting back to normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war, at least while you were working on television, did you have any problems in getting the materials you needed, for example, spare parts for your equipment?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the television was improvised as far as technology went. We had very few resources. But there were younger people, students of electronic engineering who were very bright, very capable, and they managed to improvise. We had very few resources but we had very clever people there who were able to assemble things. But there was always something lacking. Later on, when the war really started, we could see that we were short of tapes. Then we found that we should take care how we were using our tapes. And then later on, when I had already gone to the front line, I heard that my colleagues were making use of bits of tapes which were still empty tapes, re-using old tapes and so on. But when I went back to the television, the situation was critical for another two months. We would have one new tape, and we would use old ones, filming things over and over the old ones. So there were some things I was unable to preserve for the archives. When people came to ask me, I was very embarrassed, but we had to hurry and sometimes we would destroy material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions about this. The archives of the video materials that were broadcast, are they complete?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for the news reports, that's complete. It should not be damaged or destroyed. But that applies only to the news broadcasts. As for the rest of the archives, it was exposed to various kinds of damage, because if someone found three minutes of empty tape, they would put it in their camera and then they would do seven minutes, thereby destroying four minutes of something that had been filmed before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise for being too fast. Do you perhaps remember in those first few days of the conflict -- I apologise. I have to rephrase my question. Do you know Dr. Mujezinovic from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Dr. Mujezinovic, because almost everybody in Vitez knows him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember, on the first days of the conflict he made a statement on television personally?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember he did make a statement. As the only SDA politician, he was available there. He had authority as a doctor among all citizens, and he did make a statement on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember roughly what sort of statement it was, what its purpose was?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time there were a lot of rumours going around, and one of those rumours was that he had been killed or captured. So it was necessary to draw people's attention to the fact that they should not believe rumours easily without checking them. He denied the rumours that he had been killed and we wanted to broadcast this, and then he took the opportunity to call on citizens and politicians to be reasonable and to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. try to settle this situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice, when was this statement broadcast, in what programme? And was it always the same version that was broadcast?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the night the statement was filmed, it was broadcast immediately in its entirety. Perhaps later on, when it was rebroadcast, perhaps in the news broadcast or somewhere else, we rebroadcast certain things; also, on satellite television and HTV, the Croatian television. Rather, we rebroadcast things from HTV and others, and so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on what is important in this case, and let us try and speed up. We've had another 40 minutes. I thought you were going to be short this morning. Now, is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Two short questions to close this subject, and then I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conclude on the basis of anything at all or learn that Dr. Mujezinovic made the statement under duress?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We communicated with him -- rather, the people who communicated with him were his friends. He was a medical specialist. We knew each other from before and we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you. I'm sorry for being a little bit longer than predicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions for Mr. Kordic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we deal with the private session passage immediately and briefly, so that if we can have a quick private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did the Croats of Vitez imprison their Muslim friends and neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my opinion that that was a question of safety and security in the town itself, that is to say, the safety of the units in town and the safety of the people themselves who, in those chaotic days, were exposed to the possibility of maltreatment, and their lives were perhaps at risk. So for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the Croats did not need to be imprisoned, did they?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croats in town? Well, I don't know if they were imprisoned then. Whether they had to or didn't have to, I really don't know. Other people were there too --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've seen, as you tell us, one of the detention facilities of the several that were in Vitez; it contained Muslims. Are you suggesting that there was a place that had Croats detained? If so, identify the place.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In town I don't think there were places like that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- except perhaps in the Mahala, where the territory was controlled by the forces of the BH army. Probably they were there, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "probably." I want your evidence, please. So the Croats in Vitez did not need to be imprisoned for their safety. Let's return to the Muslims. From what did they need to be protected, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this chaotic state of affairs. Because at the time in town, refugees began to turn up, displaced persons, from the surroundings of Vitez, and they weren't a controlled mass. They had left their place of residence and come into town. This was a great mass of people. It was difficult for the organs of law and authority to establish effective control --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and things to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the incoming refugees, what was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats from the surrounding villages, they would come into town. That means that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the Muslims simply had to be imprisoned because incoming Croats might attack them? Is that really your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I wouldn't put it that way, I wouldn't formulate it that way, although there is some logic in it. But that's not a very happy way of putting it. The situation changed from minute to minute. It wasn't a conclusion based on constant data or a well-organised and firmly established fact. We had to adapt to the situation which changed daily. And the people who were there to assess the situation probably assessed it and concluded --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zirdum, please listen to the questions, take your time and try and give a clear answer. Staying with the same topic, you were a journalist, twice a television reporter, and you told us this yesterday - I'll quote it here so that you can remember the passage - "Information always finds a channel," that is, information always found a channel to get to you. Who decided to imprison the Croats -- the Muslims in your town?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really don't. I really don't know who took that decision, because that imprisonment began two days before I was mobilised, before I left my basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many days did you spend with these prisoners, going to and from the places they were detained? How many days were you with them?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 15 days --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can't tell you exactly. About 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can't tell us who decided to imprison the Muslims, can you tell us what the accepted reason given for their imprisonment was?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the accepted reason was to ensure law and order in town, that is to say, to ensure that incidents would not take place and some shooting from one building to another and the setting up of hundreds of front lines and, of course, general safety of those people. So that was the reason. This reason was announced to the people and, as far as I know, the people accepted that reasoning and many people asked advice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you now saying that the Muslims were imprisoned because there was fear that they might, themselves, fight or fight back; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was that fear. Before I tell you something else, may I -- could we go back into private session because I would have to mention a few names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: By way of example there would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So despite what you said earlier about being for their own protection, the imprisonment of the Muslims was because the Croats were concerned about what Muslim men might do; is that now your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult with that kind of formulation but, conditionally speaking, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the reason that the Croats of Vitez were concerned about what the Muslims might do is because the Muslims might react to the attack that was being mounted on them in Vitez and elsewhere by the Croats. That's the reality, isn't it? It's very simple.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have simplified it, but that wasn't reality. That does not reflect the reality. The reality was far more complex. Many Muslims and many Croats did not have any idea that a conflict of that kind could take place, although some people in their heads did have ideas of this kind, and probably certain circles on both sides, I assume, did look into those possibilities. The very fact that my meeting, and I don't want to mention the person that had bombs in my house whereas I didn't have any bombs, and that there were these two Croats in my entrance, I don't know why that man needed any bombs because we didn't need any weapons in town. The front line should have been against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You have described the events of the 15th, 16th, 17th and so on as appearing like, "...just an incident, just a clash." Now, Ahmici is five minutes down the road. What happened in Ahmici wasn't just an incident and it wasn't just a clash, now, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was a crime that shocked everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, information always found a way, a channel to reach you, so can you tell us, please, who --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but if this question is leading where I suppose it is leading, I will kindly ask for a private session. That is what witness asked me earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of meetings on the night of the 15th of April where Blaskic and others were present and they planned the attack on Ahmici? Did you discover about those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I heard that there had been a session of the municipal council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which, you say "a session of the municipal council," would it be right to say --

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal -- the HVO government, if you want me to be precise, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although -- did you also hear that that meeting was not attended by the actual municipal presidents or indeed, I think, the head of the defence department was attended by a selected number of people; did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. All I heard was that there was a rather dramatic session but I learned about that much later, perhaps even after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that Dario Kordic was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should really like to -- I'd really love to know more about that meeting because it must have been a very dramatic one --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Kordic was present at that meeting, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn of any later applications made by citizens of Vitez to Kordic following on that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: What application? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that citizens of Vitez went and approached Kordic later that same night, after the meeting, seeking a postponement of the attack?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I'm going to ask on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is the material on which those questions are placed? I don't remember the evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking the questions based on other material that has come to hand. Let's just deal with a few matters of generality, and then I think I don't have very much more to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as television and radio is concerned - I'm not going to take you wearisomely through the material - do you accept that the HZ HB, Herceg-Bosna, regarded the dissemination of information through television as really a State or a Herceg-Bosna business?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring here to a report on the HVO. It's Exhibit 511, and it's at page 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept, then, that the HZ HB regarded the dissemination of information through the television as partly its business?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your wording, you have to know that I was in -- on two different occasions, that is, mid-1992 and after the war of the 16th of April, the situation was quite different in both those cases. In the beginning, it was very vague. It was local. It was mixed with private business, and so on. Later on it was a business which was also to serve the purpose of the defence, that is, both information and the defence. You know, it is very difficult to give a specific answer. It is difficult to answer in the affirmative because there was one thing there and another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware -- I know you'd gone back to your factory, you say, but were you aware that in December of 1992, Exhibit 304 refers, there were talks between Dario Kordic and others about finding the best way to advance their position through radio stations? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I really am not aware of any detail dating to that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you would accept that by the time of your second involvement in television, after the outbreak in April, what you were doing was in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reality the Croats' side of things, and you were working for a Croat station; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically. Basically, yes. Basically. But again, you must distinguish it from the first few days when the situation was different and when some modality was being sought to try to bring things to an end. But as the things developed then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked questions about your role as an IPD officer. Only a couple of questions about that. Information and propaganda was a very wide business in the HVO, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't all that widespread, because I know all the people who are involved there. And if at some point in time I had to do it - and I was not an HDZ man and a man they particularly trusted, but I enjoyed the trust of people in the field - it means that it wasn't all that widespread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were dealing with it, was it propaganda that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was dealing with information, and I was trying to sustain the morale and discipline on the front lines so that our defence would manage, so that those men would put up with these inhumane conditions to perform the defence tasks in a disciplined manner. Because people were quite tired and exhausted, and it had to be explained that we needed to defend ourselves, that we had no other way out but to defend ourselves --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that was rather complicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were instructed by your superiors in the IPD chain to tell the troops things that would encourage them; is that about right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an inadequate term, "encouragement." That is an inadequate term. It is a very complex stage. You can't really define it by one word only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your role as an IPD officer -- I think you can confirm that every unit had an IPD officer, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There was a system which changed as it developed. So that in addition to my post as the assistant commander, from the new commander who was appointed I was given a new task, because he thought that it was how it should be organised, that there should be an IPD assistant per sector, not per company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on from that. As an IPD officer, you weren't seeing orders from the generals and the colonels of a military nature, were you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your position as an IPD officer, you weren't able to say anything about the overall strategy or tactics of the war, because you were simply there to encourage the troops at a local level; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- no, no, no, no, that's not how it was. In our chain of command, we had our briefings with the brigade assistant for IPD; he would transmit information to us. But I am a man from the media, and people in the field thought that I knew how to follow up on information and that I knew the extent of information they needed in the situation. Any wartime situation, you know, when chaos sets in, when people want to be informed, then simply people in the field, on the ground, trusted me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that --

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The television that you were operating for a time, or you were a journalist for for a time, did that fall fairly and squarely within the control of the IPD department?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's yet another difficult question, but I'll do my best to answer it. The head of the information centre was a gentleman called Anto Marjanovic, and the IPD assistant of the brigade was Zvonimir Cilic. So these are two different individuals. It is difficult to explain the symbiosis there, but it functioned, conditionally speaking, independently of the IPD office even though we did cooperate, which is only natural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the politician to whom the military men were answerable in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's really difficult to answer because it's a very complex situation. Troops account to their commanders in units, of course, when everything is well organised, when everything is in working order. In the political setting, well, it's an entire setting and I explained it in my -- I explained that I joined the HVO when I realised that it was not a party army but the regular army of the Croat people. Even though there were some party armies, I always rejected that very resolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hoped I'd asked a simple question. You try and answer it, if it's capable of being answered. Who was the politician to whom the military men were answerable in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to answer that question, because military and people are one and the same, and it is difficult to differentiate between the army and the people. So you have to phrase your question differently because I cannot simply answer it specifically, since you must know that that question is very difficult to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the military and political leadership was simply merged in Central Bosnia? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO government, I never managed to really clarify all those elements. But when one says "the HVO government," or "the HVO," or "the Croat Defence Council," of course it is very complicated at the notional level. I don't know how merged it is or not. But we were satisfied that we had the HVO. And the HVO had its civilian and its military wings. How merged they were, how separated they were, I still am not quite sure today, and I really did not manage to understand it fully --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I know that it worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the worst of the fighting in April was over, the leadership of Central Bosnia announced, didn't it, to the listening and viewing public that the Croats had, as it were, defeated the Muslims. It was presented as a victory.

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any such statement; absolutely no statement mentioning the words "victory" or "defeat."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were announcing the position of the Croats at that time were Kordic, Blaskic, and probably the man Kostroman as well; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, yes. Even though there were other people there, Valenta and, what do you know, other people at the time while I still attended press conferences, and they informed the public about the situation as a whole. Others also did that. But this was the most complete information for the whole region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was clear to you, was it, that Kordic, Kostroman, and Blaskic represented that merged political-military leadership, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the form of that question. To be fair to the witness, I think that he said that he did not know whether the HVO, in his view, the civilian and political wings, were merged, and the question intimates that he has actually conceded that they were merged. That's not the case. So I think to be fair to the witness, the question should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question can be put perfectly fairly: Did Kordic, Kostroman, and Blaskic represent a merged political-military leadership? That, of course, is the Prosecution case, and the Prosecutor is entitled to put it. Now, the witness has had time to think. What is the answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is, even though they were physically present and cooperating, they did not [as interpreted] have quite separated spheres of operation, because Kordic would speak about the political situation, Blaskic about the military one. But naturally you have all the material and you could follow these sessions. So it was quite clear when I attended those sessions, that was how it was. And then Kostroman would appear for operative matters, and Valenta as the deputy prime minister, and each one would cover his own area of work in those sessions, while I followed those sessions, those press conferences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. Interpreter's mistake. "They did have quite separate spheres of operation," not "did not have."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of other matters of detail. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we noticed a substantial mistake in the transcript. It is page 32, line 24. There is the quotation. "They did not have quite separate ..." The witness clearly said, "They did have quite separated ..." There was no negation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreter has corrected that already, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the reporter on the ground, Mr. Zirdum, who was responsible for the Vitez truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure, but I think it was a special purpose unit, the Vitezovi. But I heard that very unofficially, very much off the record, and I am not aware of any particular details that I would speak about. But somewhere in the town something was being done, and there are some assumptions -- there were those assumptions from which I drew this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bodies from Ahmici that were taken out by lorry before they were eventually buried in Stari Vitez, where did those bodies go before they were buried? You were there. Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. I do not know that. I do know that I was present when one had talk -- there was a hodza from Mahala there, he had come to the negotiations. We, the journalists, were in front of the door but we did not -- we were not able to learn anything. We only learnt about the exchange. So I really don't know about that, and I must say I didn't really give it a thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't give a thought to the fact that the large number of bodies from Ahmici were in some way collected up by lorry and moved around before they were buried; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, that is what I am saying. You know, you simply don't have time to think about certain things when too many things happen simultaneously and later on, perhaps, you can think about this. But at that time, one simply didn't even try to think where was what because there was simply no time to systematically keep up with all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man you spoke of yesterday as not being a strong man, Suad Salkic, why was he taken to Kaonik, a friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that he was taken to Kaonik. I think I saw him after the war and gave him some things of his. We did meet but we were never one on one. We never really could discuss it, but I don't know that he was there. And about him, yes, indeed, I should have known. I should have been aware had he been taken to Kaonik. I would have known that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us you were dealing with the prisoners on a regular basis. Why were any of them taken to Kaonik, please? Why was it necessary for the Croats to take their Muslim neighbours to the prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very little about Kaonik. It was only in the course of the war that I learned of existence and I understood that they were taking there, those Croat soldiers who had committed some disciplinary transgressions. It was much later that I learned that there was a prison at Kaonik, that there were Mujahedin there. But I found out about that when the exchange of Zivko Totic for those Mujahedin took a place. Then that is where I found out that there was some Mujahedin there. Until that time, I didn't even know of its existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about the grouping of which Suad Salkic was a member. Do you remember a woman named Vildana Sanjic who was also a member of that group of intellectuals and she was --

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Vildana. Vildana but you got her surname wrong, and I'm not quite sure about it, but there was a Vildana who worked with us at the television at that time when I worked there, the first two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. And she was sacked because she was a Muslim, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess she must have expressed her solidarity. She was one of that rare category of assistants who expressed their solidarity with me and several journalists, that is, he could stay with those cameramen and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that she lost her job because she was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right because it was an experiment then. There wasn't really proper job there. People had not yet -- they did not have their labour contracts yet and it is early, I was still involved in this technical organisation, coordination and such like. And will you just give me precisely the name of Vildana because I've forgotten it, and I hope we are referring to one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring to the person on the television. You seem to accept that she lost her job, and I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've only got a couple of questions that I'd like to finish by the break, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were sometimes in the Workers' University HVO press centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. It was the information centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember being there on an occasion in April 1993 when a precision mechanic had been called in to deal with some machinery and a typewriter at a time when it was thought that the mosque in the village of Preocica had been successfully targeted; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, and I don't see what does it have to do with the mosque in the village of Preocica. And I don't know you are mentioning March, April. Your question is completely vague, confused, imprecise and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for you to comment. You are here as a witness, Mr. Zirdum, and to give answers. Now, we'll get on more quickly if you simply answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, I'm going to suggest to you that in the circumstances --

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies to the Court and to the Prosecutor, but he really asked me a very complicated and a very confused question and I simply failed to understand it. I am trying to understand it, not to ask you to repeat it, in order to resolve it more quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am suggesting to you that on the occasion that I have identified, you and others were enjoying or glorying in the understanding that the mosque in Preocica had been attacked and that you were overheard in the sentence by a precision mechanic that had been summoned to that building. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that. I have no idea about any mosque in any Preocica being targeted, and I do not think that anyone on my team would rejoice at that. I am talking about my team in the press centre. Perhaps somewhere else in some other centre there may be people who rejoiced and gloated over that but we certainly did not. And especially nobody would gloat over that in front of a mechanic who was of Muslim, Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've spoken about Dr. Mujezinovic. You weren't present when he was spoken, if he was, by Cerkez before he made that television broadcast were you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there. I did not see them communicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot say whether he was pressed or pressured into making that broadcast. You simply don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that there was any pressure put on him in my presence in the offices of the press service of those information. I guarantee that there was nothing like that. It was a very civilised and friendly discussion because Marijanovic, my friend and I, we all cooperated. There was no pressure there. Whether there was any pressure before that, whether he'd been anywhere before that and if he talked to anyone else, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one simple question in order to clarify one thing which was -- I'm sorry, just a short question more to clarify one issue. Re-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zirdum, at the very beginning of your cross-examination, you were asked about the detention of Muslims and non-detention of Croats. You do not have to give us any value judgements but please try to answer me as briefly as possible. In your opinion, on the 16th of April, who was it that attacked the town?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view -- well, I can't do it briefly, but the Muslim forces from the direction of Zenica seemed to have already been prepared, but in that part, they must have been attacking already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned shelling, and the shells were coming from where?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it, shells were coming from Vjetrenica, tank shells were coming from Vjetrenica for several days, and I remember that resolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what forces were defending the town? What army was there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the -- the town was defended by citizens of Vitez, I simply know that for several days, there were calls being sent, I mean, "Whoever can come, come."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the defendants of the town were Croats, is it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you think of any reason why, under the circumstances, that the Croats could be imprisoned for the safety of the town?

utterances.speaker: ANTO ZIRDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirdum, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for half an hour. 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before the witness is sworn, there is one matter of the Court's arrangements that I want to deal with. Apparently on Friday there is likely to be some sort of action by fuel truck drivers or truck drivers in The Hague and, as a result, it may well affect the ability of the transport police to get the accused here. We have a hearing in another case which is scheduled for Friday and in view of those difficulties, we are minded to move that hearing to tomorrow afternoon, but I just want to be sure that we can get through this case, what we have in this case, before then. Mr. Kovacic, how many witnesses have you got?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have just two witnesses left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The one which is just here presumably will be relatively short, and the next one is a bit longer but not very.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we should be able to finish comfortably by lunchtime tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that being so, we will adjourn this case then and we'll make arrangements for the other case to be heard at 3.00 on Thursday. Thank you. Yes, let the witness be sworn, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Tibold.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On behalf of the Defence of Mario Cerkez, I will conduct your examination-in-chief. Please try to recall the events as best you can that we will discuss and please take into account the needs of the interpreters and wait before answering my questions and speak a little more slowly than usual. Mr. Tibold, please introduce yourself with your full name and the year and place of your birth.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: My name is Zdenko Tibold. I was born on the 3rd of September 1952 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you lived in Vitez all your life?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a Croat by nationality, Roman Catholic?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have dual nationality; you are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are a bank clerk by profession?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the moment, you are employed in Zagrebacka Banka of Bosnia-Herzegovina with its seat in Mostar and there is a branch office in your native town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You finished high school?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the army in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you acquire any rank?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: I was a corporal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which party?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: The HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you hold any post in the political party, any duty?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Not now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have two brothers?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of your brothers is Dr. Tibold, also from Vitez? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tibold, if I'm right, you finished high school in 1976?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you get your first job?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were employed?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: In the bank Privredna Banka Sarajevo, the branch office in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since that time in 1976 until today, you have been in the banking business?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are an eyewitness to all the monetary events to say from then until today, both in the former Yugoslavia and today in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The branch office of the Sarajevo bank in Vitez, it was transformed into the Travnik bank Privredna Banka at one point?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember who, in 1992, was the director of the branch office in which you were employed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: In 1992, it was Mr. Velimir Didak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What nationality is he?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of the employees in the bank in which you were employed, the Privredna Banka Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Mostly Croats and Muslims, and there were some Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could it be said then that it was a Croatian or a Muslim or some other bank with respect to ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: A bank is a bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tibold, until what time was that branch office operating in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: I left it in the beginning of 1992, and it continued operating until approximately the end of that year when there was an explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was damaged in that explosion?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, that explosive device was planted on the outside. It destroyed the whole premises of the bank, and it was very difficult to continue operating in that bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, in fact, the bank closed down?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other banks at that time operating in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: No, there were no banks functioning in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were payments made then when there was no bank; through what institution?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, it was the payment transfer service or the SDK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tibold, was a police investigation conducted about the explosive device planted in the bank and the damage it caused?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: I assume it was, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume then that you do not know whether it was established who perpetrated that attack?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Not to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tibold, in your banking circles, what did people say? Whose interest was it to plant an explosive device in the bank?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, all the time people said it could have been done by someone who owed the bank money, whether it was a loan or whether it was a current account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that, in that explosion, the bank documentation, the records were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Most of them, yes, because a fire broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tibold, you have told us that after this explosion and before that, no other banks operated in Vitez. Was there talk of preparations for the opening of another bank in the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes. We were working on that, and I was to go over to the Privredna Banka Zagreb, and I did. I left the Privredna Banka Travnik in early 1992, but that bank never actually started work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tibold, did that bank already have some premises in Vitez where it was supposed to start operating?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes. The premises were set up and everything was ready for the bank to open up, however, that never happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did it never happen?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Because of the political options and because of the military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please allow me to explain something before I go on. The witness Tibold arrived in The Hague yesterday evening at about 9.00 p.m. and brought with him two short documents which are relevant for these proceedings and his testimony. These documents, unfortunately, could not be translated in this brief period of time. I would like to adduce them into evidence in these proceedings, and I would ask that they be translated, briefly, by the interpreters and then official translation can be made later. The translating booths have these documents and I think this can be done very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The document can be put on the ELMO so we can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel must read the documents out loud, or the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be document D110/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tibold, this is the document you gave me yesterday. We see that it is an order issued by the Vitez -- HVO Vitez Defence office and it was signed by Mr. Marijan Skopljak who was the head of the defence office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now read only the first and second item. It says, "For the needs of the HVO government in Vitez, the premises of the Privredna Banka Zagreb with their seat in Vitez are being temporarily set aside." And item two, "The person responsible for handing over the premises is Zdenko Tibold and for the reception, Josip Silic." Mr. Tibold, very briefly, can you comment on this document? What is this about?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, this is about the handing over of the premises of Zagrebacka Banka for the needs of the defence office of Travnik with its headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So to put it more simply, these premises were requisitioned for the needs of the defence office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tibold, after you stopped working in the Travnik Privredna Banka, you did a job on a part-time basis. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, I was the treasurer of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tibold, can we please go back to the year 1992 at the time when the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared its independence. When it declared its independence, did Bosnia and Herzegovina introduce its national currency immediately?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What currency, at that moment, was in use in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the declaration of independence?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: There was the Yugoslav dinar, the Croatian dinar, the German mark and other currencies. But those three were the main ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Yugoslav dinar, of course, it is quite clear to us why it remained in use. It was there and there were no possibilities of withdrawing it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The German mark is the currency of a quite different country. How did it come about that it was used in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: The German mark was the only currency that the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised, regardless of whether they were Muslims, Croats, or Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the situation the same in the former Yugoslavia before its dissolution?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes, because most people who worked abroad and who came from Vitez and other places, they worked in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the situation the same today that the German mark is used in parallel with the official currency?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Yugoslav dinar existed as a currency in that area. How did people accept it; was it a currency that was accepted, that was used? What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: The Yugoslav dinar was a currency which remained in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was used until other currencies turned up; however, the Yugoslav dinar appeared in large quantities so, in fact, you couldn't use it to buy something because inflation was terrible, and everybody avoided the Yugoslav dinar. People who travelled used the German mark because it was the only currency accepted in the western market and those who travelled to Croatia and further on also used the Croatian dinar which was later transformed into the Croatian kuna because it was the only currency that could be used in Croatia to the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now ask the usher ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D111/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The other side. The other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tibold, tell us, what sort of note is this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: This is a note of the Yugoslav state of 1993 for 500 billion dinars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was one of the currencies in use in that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: This currency was used in Yugoslavia; as for Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was for smaller amounts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help us to understand this enormous sum? What could you buy for it? In general, was that a large value?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: I don't know about Yugoslavia. I think it wasn't. But in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1991, 880.000 Yugoslav dinars were equivalent to 100 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As inflation grew, did this relationship become even worse?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tibold, we are still talking about mid-1992. I would ask the registrar -- yes, we have a number. Thank you. So we are talking about the aggression of the JNA and the Bosnian Serb army on the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The city of Sarajevo was under siege; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo were the government bodies.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was that situation reflected in the dissemination or the distribution of the national currency?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult. It was very difficult to establish any kind of communication or transfer of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was that the reason why the German mark was used more and more, and later on the Croatian dinar or kuna?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, everyone in the Vitez municipality and the Lasva River Valley, all enterprises worked independently to preserve the value of their goods or their currency. So the municipality of Travnik at that time issued a voucher which was used on the territory of Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This voucher printed by the municipality, was this regulated by government legislation, or was it a decision on the part of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: It was printed by the bank; it was issued by the bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes, within the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This voucher was supposed to replace money as currency for payments.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tibold, you said that the town of Travnik issued vouchers. Were they valid in other towns; for example, in Vitez, in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: It was valid on the territory of Vitez but not on the territory of Zenica. Zenica had their own vouchers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, in fact, that certain areas or certain towns on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in fact, had their own vouchers which they used to make payments?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. That was a transitional period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For you as a bank clerk, what sort of situation was this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: It was ridiculous, I have to admit. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But very briefly, please. What difficulties did you have, you as an ordinary citizen, in the use of these vouchers and other currencies at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Well, as a bank clerk I had problems with people who had savings accounts, because they demanded hard currency and there was none available. All we could give them were Yugoslav dinars or vouchers and they could be used only in that area. As time passed by, in 1992 people didn't want vouchers either because they couldn't use them to buy goods, so that those who had large amounts of Yugoslav dinars and vouchers would simply go bankrupt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tibold, if you travelled from Vitez to Zenica, you had to have vouchers from Zenica which you could not obtain in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: That's correct. We had to change them for German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in fact it was more practical to take German marks with you in the first place.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During all this time, that is to say, 1992, the end of it, and the beginning of 1993, in the Republic of Croatia the currency at the time which was called the dinar and, later on, the kuna, was present, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said that that currency came to your regions for the reasons you've mentioned. Was it accepted, the Croatian kuna, in exchanges, daily exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: In time, yes, with the passage of time. At the beginning, less so until trade with Croatia began to develop, because we could only obtain goods from Croatia. As transactions increased and traffic increased, the towns that were closer to Croatia, salaries were no longer calculated in dinars but were calculated in kunas or in German marks. I apologise. Not kunas, but Croatian dinars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The kuna was introduced later on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tibold, according to your recollections and your personal experience as a bank clerk, at any time did any authority in the municipality, or at any other level, bring in provisions according to which just one currency was allowed in transactions?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to take a look at the last document you gave me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D112/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a communication issued by the HVO government in Vitez and signed by Ivan Santic, the president of the Vitez HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This communique was issued after a session of the 24th of August, 1992, in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read item I: "On the territory of the municipality of Vitez, it shall be possible to use in the transfer of payments all currencies, including the Bosnian dinar as currency." Does this correspond to your recollection and your experience at that time, Mr. Tibold?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tibold, we heard a few days ago testimony in which a person said that at the Kalem gas pump in Vitez, in the morning gasoline was sold for Bosnian dinars, and in the afternoon the owner refused to sell it for Bosnian dinars but only for German marks. Are you surprised by this?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you perhaps yourself a witness to similar events in shops, in banks, and in general where money was used?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Everyone in the area of the Lasva area used the currency they wanted to use, everything was in use. I have to admit that when the Yugoslav dinar was changed to the Bosnian dinar, the ratio was 1:1, later it was 1:3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The Bosnian dinar, after being introduced at the end of 1992, remained a legal tender up until what time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Up until the time it was changed to the convertible mark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your introduction that, despite that, the German mark continued to be a parallel source of payment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for you, Mr. Tibold. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO TIBOLD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Kordic Defence has no questions to put to this witness. Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:
